Native connected machines

Native connected-machine adapter using the existing Codex Desktop registration.

About 9 min read · 11 sections

On this page
01 Verified app engines 02 Relay sessions and native chats 03 Project trust on mobile 04 Activation 05 Session diagnostics 06 Stream ends 07 Transport counters 08 Lost-request detection 09 Reset switch 10 Reading the logs 11 Build and checks

The native relay sits in front of the gateway's app-server router. It uses the same environment ID, installation ID, server name, account, and client-name scope as the machine's existing Codex Desktop registration. It does not create another machine or require an SSH entry in the desktop UI.

The adapter is included in managed GateFox releases. Keep each Mac's existing registration and confirm its live state with gateway rollout --verify --json; installation alone does not prove readiness. Earlier prototype results and version-specific checks are recorded in verification.

The SDK reads host authentication from the native account through its normal auth manager. Authentication is never copied into the relay home. Inference still uses the gateway's separately registered providers. Only the original registration's metadata is read from the primary SQLite database, through a read-only connection. The relay keeps its own database and preferences in a private home. Native config, transcripts, and SQLite files are not migrated or rewritten by registration.

The relay refuses a missing, disabled, or differently owned registration. Its SDK build blocks creating replacement enrollments.

Choose setup and builds or troubleshooting for focused instructions.

Verified app engines

The relay remains linked to the Codex SDK released as rust-v0.163.0-alpha.10.2. The accepted engines retain the remote-control wire contract, so the relay can keep that linked SDK. Earlier accepted 0.162/0.163 engines have byte-identical app-server-transport source. The relay and the shared native host keep separate lists in src/native-engine-versions.ts:

App engine Relay (relayAcceptedAppEngines) Shared native host (hostVerifiedAppEngines)

codex-cli 0.167.0-alpha.3.2 Requires the rebuilt relay (1.7.7); app-server-transport, state migrations and the auth.json format unchanged from 0.166.0-alpha.6 Verified with the signed engine through the stdio and Unix shared-native fixtures, with and without --host-codex (8 Nov 2026, 1.7.8)

See desktop update compatibility for startup diagnostic passthrough, app-bundle replacement isolation and the 0.164 review.

The 0.163.0-alpha.11.2, 0.163.0-alpha.11.1, 0.163.0-alpha.11, 0.163.0-alpha.10.2, and 0.162.0-alpha.17.2 releases ship a byte-identical app-server-transport crate, so the remote-control protocol, the patched stream-end hooks, the existing-registration guard and the remoteControl/* methods are the same for these app engines. The 0.163 state database adds two migrations, and the SDK opens a database that a newer release migrated, so a rollback to a 0.162 relay still opens the relay home.

The 11.2 comparison covered all 36 app-server-transport files, which matched 11.1 and the linked 10.2 source byte for byte. Its signature and reported version were checked on the M5 before the isolated shared-native fixture ran. The fixture used no copied authentication or paid inference and left no owned SDK process behind. This compatibility admission requires a newly built relay; changing the TypeScript list alone cannot update an older installed relay binary.

Shared-engine verification covers more than the protocol. In 0.163, pending unloads became a map with a wake-up signal, listener removal now checks the thread's generation, finished v2 sub-agent threads unload automatically, and startup configuration resolves against the working directory. The 0.163 fixture also verifies every frontend disappearing during inference or a pending approval, followed by recovery of the same SDK process, turn, history, and original approval request. An engine joins hostVerifiedAppEngines only after scripts/e2e-shared-native.mjs passes against it. The relay needs none of that, because it never uses the host's engine (see the next section).

The relay's own list is native-relay/src/cli_version.rs; a gateway test fails when it differs from relayAcceptedAppEngines. The relay compares the text that the app CLI prints for --version; it does not check the code signature itself. Its --codex path is the app's own launcher, taken from the service plan or the registration, and a host that shares an engine verifies OpenAI's signature (TeamIdentifier 2DC432GLL2) before it runs it. Gateway chats are a separate pin: they run the release's own gateway SDK (0.162.0-alpha.17.2), whatever engine the app ships. A relay that refuses the app's engine exits at once, and after three such exits the service sets it aside with component_paused and reason failing instead of restarting it in a loop. A new app engine needs a new relay build and this verification again.

Every stop now logs its reason on the line before Native relay stopped; private state retained: one of the relay's own fixed refusals, such as Native relay requires the matching Codex CLI build or Another relay owns this native server, or a coarse class for anything else. Paths, accounts and values are never printed.

The relay reads the original machine registration from the native database with /usr/bin/sqlite3 -readonly. A service restart stops every engine that has that database open, and the next opener recovers or checkpoints its WAL under an exclusive lock. Without a busy timeout the read failed at once with database is locked, so the new relay exited about 30 ms after Native relay host authenticated, three times in a row, and paused for half an hour (MacBook Pro, 31 Oct 2026). The read now waits up to five seconds for the lock and retries a failed run twice, one second apart. A missing or disabled registration is an answer, not a failure, and is still refused at once.

Relay sessions and native chats

Each phone stream starts its own gateway codex-shim session, so the model list, the chat list and the routing the phone sees are the gateway router's. The relay answers only remoteControl/* itself; thread/list, model/list and turns go to the router.

Native chats run where any adapter runs them. When the host shares the native engine, the session attaches to it. Otherwise the session's adapter runs a private native engine on the native home: always on a plan with sharedNativeExecutor: false, and as a fallback when the host cannot share the app's engine. From 0.4.7, private engines share the native home with each other, so the app's adapter and the relay's sessions each run one. The ChatGPT app opened after the relay connected leaves remote control to the relay.

One chat still has one writer. The SDK keeps a per-chat writer lock in <native home>/thread-writer-locks: while the app's engine holds a native chat, the phone's thread/resume is refused with already has an active writer, and once the app lets the chat go (it closes the chat's engine, for example by quitting), the phone continues it. Gateway chats use the host when the plan shares gateway executors, and otherwise private gateway engines under the same lock.

Project trust on mobile

A project appearing in the picker does not prove that its original folder has a saved trust decision. This affects both new chats and existing chats. A trusted child repository does not trust its parent folder, and a projects."/" entry is not a wildcard. Mobile can refuse the turn before turn/start, with "Can't verify project trust". Check the native engine's config/read response with the selected cwd and includeLayers: true; use the native user layer, not a gateway executor's private configuration snapshot.

An operator who wants all selected folders trusted can explicitly set "trustAllProjects": true in that machine's gateway configuration. This is off by default and applies when an adapter process loads that configuration. Existing listeners keep their loaded choice until they retire normally. The adapter saves real, version-guarded native trust entries for registered project roots and requested working directories. New project creation and chat start/resume/fork also establish trust before the result reaches the client or the chat loads. Gateway executors receive the same policy in their own private configuration, so an older snapshot does not lose the choice. Existing aliases are resolved and both spellings are trusted, so a canonical untrusted entry cannot defeat the selected folder's trust. Starts without a working directory use the engine's reported default before loading settings. A shared host from an older release that cannot report its default requires an explicit folder for such a start until that host upgrades normally.

This policy accepts every selected folder, including a folder previously marked untrusted. Repository instructions, project configuration and enabled hooks may therefore load automatically. Command approval and sandbox settings remain the caller's choices. The adapter returns the engine's actual configuration and layer provenance; a managed override or failed write remains a failure. It does not manufacture a trusted response or start a separate maintenance job.

Clearing the flag stops automatic trust after the adapter processes reload. Trust decisions already saved remain in Codex's user configuration until the operator changes them. A gateway release that predates this option must first adopt a release that implements it; editing configuration alone cannot add the behavior.

Run node scripts/e2e-project-trust.mjs --root /tmp/TASK/project-trust to verify the policy through the signed native engine and both adapter execution paths. The fixture uses private homes, a local model catalog and one localhost mock turn, with no external provider inference.
